symptom: `mxcli test --local` hangs indefinitely on Windows after the tests finish, when mxbuild starts a new Gradle daemon — no results, no JUnit file, no error; a run that reuses an idle daemon passes, and killing only the orphaned daemon unblocks mxcli (#1396). `mx sync-java-dependencies` (run --local) has the same shape
cause: `mxbuild --serve` and `mx sync-java-dependencies` write to a `syncBuffer`, so exec.Cmd creates a pipe and Wait blocks until every holder of its write end closes it. A freshly started Gradle daemon inherits that end and outlives mxbuild; the tree kill (taskkill /T, or the POSIX group signal) cannot reach a process that left the tree/group, and `ServeServer.Stop` runs before results are printed
file: `cmd/mxcli/docker/mxserve.go` (`newServeCmd`, `orphanPipeWaitDelay`), `cmd/mxcli/docker/javadeps.go` (`SyncJavaDependencies` treats `exec.ErrWaitDelay` as success — mx's own exit status wins)
insight: `cmd.WaitDelay` is the backstop for EVERY exec.Cmd whose child can spawn Gradle and whose output is not an *os.File, not only the watchdogged one-shot builds (sibling finding 2026-10-11): a tree kill bounds the tree, WaitDelay bounds what escaped it. The delay starts only after the process exits, so it cannot cut a live build short. The discriminating detail in the report was 'only when no idle daemon can be reused' — a reused daemon never held this run's pipe. Reproduces on Linux with a fake mx that starts `setsid sleep 30 &` (out of the process group, like the escaped daemon); revert proof: without WaitDelay both tests block past their 15s guard
